 New report shows ‘fewer people need treatment,’ but record dengue cases, funding shortages and uneven progress threaten global disease control efforts Beyza Binnur Donmez 04 November 2026 • Update : 04 November 2026 GENEVA A total of 63 countries eliminated at least one neglected tropical disease by June 2026, but funding shortages and uneven progress threaten further gains, the World Health Organization said Wednesday.
 In its latest report, the WHO said the number of countries that eliminated at least one neglected tropical disease, or NTD, increased from 42 in 2020 to 63 by June 2026.
 A midterm assessment of the agency's 2021-2030 NTD road map found that more countries were eliminating these diseases and "fewer people need treatment."
 The number of people requiring treatment or other interventions declined to 1.41 billion in 2024, representing a 36% reduction since 2010, according to the report.
 Cases of sleeping sickness fell by 98% since 1999, while Guinea worm disease reached a historic low of 10 human cases in 2025.
 "Elimination of neglected tropical diseases is one of the standout success stories of global health," WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said.
 However, he warned that the "fragile" progress could be reversed without sustained financing and stronger integration of disease control into primary healthcare.
 Record dengue cases, funding shortages threaten gains
 Despite improvements in several areas, dengue infections reached a record 15.1 million in 2024, the WHO said.
 Efforts to eradicate yaws, another neglected tropical disease, also remain behind schedule.
 The agency found that resources for neglected tropical disease programs remained 30% below pre-pandemic levels.
 Nearly 80% of international development assistance for these programs between 2018 and 2024 came from a small group of donors, leaving disease control efforts vulnerable to sudden funding cuts.
 The WHO called for increased domestic investment, broader international donor support and faster action to meet global disease control targets by 2030.
